# How to Draft a Short, Kind Message to a Teacher or Landlord About a Problem

> **In short:** Open any AI assistant, describe your situation in plain words, and ask for a short, kind message you can send by email or text. Read the draft out loud and tweak anything that doesn't sound like you.

Sending a message to a teacher or landlord about a problem is one of those small tasks that feels awkward — you don't want to sound too pushy, too apologetic, or too vague. By the end of this short guide, you'll have a respectful message you can copy, tweak, and send in a few minutes — written with help from any AI assistant, which can suggest wording quickly but can't read your mind.

## Before you start
- Any AI assistant on phone, tablet, or laptop — free plans work for a short message
- About 10 minutes and a few honest sentences about your situation

## Step 1 — Open an AI assistant and start a new chat
Open any AI assistant you already use on your phone or laptop. Common free options you can use in a browser include ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat and DeepSeek — you don't have to install anything new.

Tap or click the **"New chat"** button, usually at the top of the sidebar or as a big box on the home screen. A blank chat window opens with a single text field at the bottom, often labeled something like "Message" or "Ask anything", though yours may say slightly different words.

The assistant is now waiting for your first instruction. You don't need to sign in again if the app is already open.

💬 Example: type a starter line like `Help me write a short message` and wait for the reply before adding detail in Step 2.

You'll know it worked when a blank text field appears and the assistant shows it's ready, often shown by an active **Send** button or a blinking cursor.

## Step 2 — Tell it your situation in plain words
In the same text field, type a short description of what's going on. Include who is involved, what happened, when it happened, and how it made you feel. Don't worry about grammar yet — just tell it the facts as you'd tell a friend.

The assistant reads your message and forms a reply within seconds. You'll see text appear word by word, or a complete answer pop in after a short pause, depending on the app.

If you see a "thinking…" indicator instead of an answer, that's normal — wait a few seconds. If the assistant asks a clarifying question, just answer honestly and keep going.

💬 Example: `My landlord hasn't fixed the broken heater in my apartment for two weeks. It's getting cold and I've sent two texts already. I want to ask for a timeline without sounding angry.`

You'll know it worked when the assistant acknowledges your situation and either drafts a message or asks one or two quick clarifying questions first.

## Step 3 — Ask for the tone and length you need
Tell the assistant how you want the message to sound. Most assistants let you ask for things like "shorter", "more apologetic", "warmer", or "more formal". A short follow-up instruction works better than rewriting everything yourself.

After you send it, the assistant rewrites the message and shows a new version. Both versions stay in the same chat, so you can compare them side by side.

If the new version still doesn't feel right, send another short instruction rather than starting over — the assistant adjusts from the last version. If your assistant has no "rewrite" or "regenerate" button, just type a new instruction in the same box.

💬 Example: `Make it shorter, around 70 words, and a little warmer in tone — keep the ask at the end.` The assistant will produce a tighter version that still sounds respectful.

You'll know it worked when a second message appears in the chat that reads closer to how you'd actually talk to the person.

## Step 4 — Read the draft out loud before you send it
Take a breath and read the draft out loud, the way you'd say it in person. This step catches things a silent read misses — a message that looks fine on screen can sound stiff or awkward when spoken.

You'll probably find one or two phrases that don't sound like you. Common offenders are formal phrases like "I would appreciate", "kindly", or "at your earliest convenience" — swap them for words you'd actually use.

If a sentence still feels wrong after one rewrite, just type `Rephrase this one sentence:` followed by the sentence in quotes. The assistant will rework only that line and leave the rest of the message intact.

💬 Example: `Rephrase this one sentence: "I would appreciate your prompt attention to this matter."` A typical reply might suggest something like "Could you let me know when I can expect this to be fixed?"

You'll know it worked when the whole message sounds like something you'd actually say — clear, calm, and respectful.

## Step 5 — Pick the right channel and send it
Decide whether to send by email or text. Email is usually better for landlords and teachers because it creates a written record you can refer back to. A short text message is fine when the situation is small and you already have an open chat with the person.

If you choose email, copy the draft from the AI chat and paste it into a new email. Add a clear subject line like "Heating repair — follow-up" — the AI can draft this too if you ask.

If you choose text, shorten the draft to two or three sentences, since long texts can feel heavy. Send the message, then put your phone down — you don't need an instant reply.

💬 Example: `Write a short subject line for this email.` The assistant will offer a few options like "Heating issue — request for update" that you can copy straight into the subject field.

You'll know it worked when the message is sent, the subject line matches the content, and you feel okay re-reading it one more time before walking away.

## Step 6 — Save what worked for next time
Once the message is sent and you're happy with the result, save the instructions that produced it. Most assistants let you name a chat, star it, or copy a share link — use whichever your app offers.

If your assistant has no built-in save feature, copy the situation paragraph and the follow-up instructions into a notes app under a heading like "Messages that worked". Next time, paste them as your starting point and adjust.

Saving good prompts means you don't have to figure out the wording from scratch each time. Over a few months, you'll build a small library of message templates that match your natural voice.

💬 Example: name the saved chat `Heater follow-up — landlord` so you can find it instantly the next time something similar comes up.

You'll know it worked when you can find the saved chat or note within ten seconds and the wording still sounds like you when you read it back.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking for a "professional" message and skipping the read-aloud.** AI defaults to formal language that often reads stiff. The fix: in Step 4, read the draft out loud and swap any word you wouldn't actually say.
- **Forgetting to include the specific detail.** A generic message like "Please fix the issue soon" won't get a useful reply. The fix: include exact dates, the item, or the problem in Step 2 — the assistant can't invent those for you.
- **Sending the first draft without asking for a rewrite.** The first version is rarely the best one. The fix: always do at least one follow-up ask like "shorter" or "warmer" in Step 3, and one sentence-level rephrase in Step 4.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** next time you have to chase a landlord about a repair, ask a teacher for an extension, or follow up on a delayed delivery, you can turn a 10-minute worry into a 2-minute task by describing the situation in plain words.
- **For your work or business:** the same habit helps with harder messages too — asking a client for payment, declining a meeting politely, or following up on a slow response. Once you trust the pattern, you can use it for any short message that feels awkward to write from scratch.
- **If you're just getting started:** keep this guide's 💬 examples handy. The first time you try it, copy one of them almost word-for-word. By the third time, you'll naturally adjust the wording to your own voice without thinking about it.

## Try it now
Pick the next small awkward message you've been putting off — a quick note to a teacher about a missed deadline, or a short follow-up to a landlord about a repair. Open any AI assistant, paste in this prompt, and spend two minutes on it: `Help me write a short, kind message. The situation is: [one or two sentences]. I want it to sound calm and respectful, around 60 words.` Read the reply out loud, tweak one phrase, and send it.
